content.title: Sales, Revenue and Costs

sections.title: Sales Volume and Sales Revenue
sections.keyIdea: Sales volume is how many units are sold; sales revenue is what they were sold for. Revenue is price multiplied by volume, so the two can move in opposite directions.

body.text: **Sales volume** counts things. **Sales revenue** counts money. The specification lists them together and it lists them as two calculations, because a firm that reports "sales are up" has told you nothing until you know which one it meant.
**Sales revenue = selling price × sales volume.** Melaka Bottling sells bottled fruit drink by the case at $6. At 20,000 cases a month its revenue is $120,000.

Because revenue is a product of two numbers, a change in one can be undone by a change in the other. Sell 24,000 cases at $5.40 and the volume is up by a fifth while the revenue is $129,600 — up by only $9,600. Sell 24,000 at $4.80 and the volume is up a fifth while the revenue has FALLEN to $115,200.
So the two questions a firm asks are different questions: how many can we sell, and what will we take for them. Everything in this chapter is one or the other.

realExample.text: A juice bottler that wins a supermarket listing reports a jump in volume and a fall in revenue per case at the same time, because the listing was won on price. Both statements are about the same quarter.

sections.misconception: Students treat "sales" as one number, so a question about improving sales revenue gets an answer about selling more units. Read which of the two the question names: they are separate calculations and a firm can raise one while lowering the other.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Calculate as requiring a calculation based on given data, with workings shown. Show the multiplication, not only the product: $6 × 20,000 is the working and $120,000 is the answer.

recall.prompt: One month the plant took $117,000 at $6.50 a case. Work back:
template: Sales volume that month was ___ thousand cases
At the usual $6 the same money would need a volume of ___ thousand
So the higher price needed ___ cases for the same revenue
hints: divide the money by the price
the same money at the lower price
compare the two volumes

sections.title: Fixed and Variable Costs
sections.keyIdea: A fixed cost does not change when output changes; a variable cost does. The split is a statement about a period of time, not about the kind of cost.

body.text: A **fixed cost** does not change when output changes. Melaka Bottling pays $36,000 a month in rent, insurance and salaried staff whether it bottles 0 cases or 25,000.
A **variable cost** changes directly with output. Every case needs $3.60 of concentrate, bottles, caps and power. Make one more case and $3.60 more is spent; make none and none is spent.
The word that does the work in both definitions is OUTPUT. A cost is not fixed because it is large or because it arrives monthly — it is fixed because output does not move it.

And the split holds only for a stated period. Over a month the rent is fixed. Over three years the plant could move to a smaller building, and then the rent is a choice like any other. This is why chapter 3 lists "costs split cleanly in two" as an assumption rather than a fact.

realExample.text: A bottling line's electricity bill has a standing charge that arrives whether the line runs and a unit charge that only arrives when it does. One bill, and the two halves sit on different lines of the cost table.

sections.misconception: Students sort by the size or the timing of the payment — rent is monthly so it is fixed, materials arrive weekly so they are variable. The test is output: hold output at zero and ask whether the cost still has to be paid.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Explain as requiring a brief explanation of cause or effect supported by details or an example. A cost named fixed needs the reason it does not move with output, not a list of costs that usually are.

recall.prompt: Sort these into fixed and variable for one month at the plant:

groups.name: Fixed for the month
items: Factory rent
Insurance premium
Salaried supervisor
groups.why: The same amount is owed at zero output as at full output.

groups.name: Variable with output
items: Bottles and caps
Drink concentrate
Power to run the line
groups.why: One more case needs one more case worth of packaging, concentrate and power.

sections.title: Total Costs and Average Costs
sections.keyIdea: Total cost is fixed plus variable at that output. Average cost is total cost divided by output, and it falls as output rises because the fixed cost is spread wider.

body.text: **Total cost = fixed costs + total variable costs.** At 20,000 cases the plant's variable costs are $3.60 × 20,000 = $72,000, so total cost is $36,000 + $72,000 = $108,000.
**Average cost = total cost ÷ output.** At 20,000 cases that is $108,000 ÷ 20,000 = $5.40 a case.

Average cost falls as output rises, and the reason is entirely in the fixed half. The variable cost per case is $3.60 at every output. The $36,000 is what gets divided: $3.60 a case at 10,000 cases, $1.80 at 20,000, $1.44 at 25,000.

One row of the chapter's table is worth marking now. At 15,000 cases average cost is $6 — exactly the selling price. A firm whose average cost equals its price is taking in precisely what it spends, and chapter 3 calls that output the break-even point.

realExample.text: A plant running one shift instead of two has a higher cost per case than the same plant at full use. The equipment and the building cost the same either way; there are simply fewer cases to divide them between.

sections.misconception: Students say average cost falls "because of economies of scale". At this level the arithmetic is simpler and more useful: the fixed cost is being divided by a bigger number. Nothing about the variable cost per unit has changed.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Calculate as requiring workings. An average cost answer with no total cost line above it cannot be followed, because the marker cannot see which output was divided into which total.

recall.prompt: Work the plant's per-case figures at 12,000 cases:
template: Fixed cost a case is $___
Add the $3.60 variable cost and average cost is $___
That is ___ the selling price, so 12,000 cases loses money
hints: the monthly fixed costs over the output
the two per-case figures together
compare it with $6.00

sections.title: Ways of Improving Sales Volumes
sections.keyIdea: Volume is raised by giving more buyers a reason to buy: a lower price, a wider distribution, a change to the product, or promotion that reaches people who had not considered it.

body.text: Raising **volume** means selling more cases. Four routes, and they are not equally available to every firm.

items: **Lower the price.** The most direct route and the one with a cost attached, which is the next subsection.
**Widen distribution.** The same product in more places: a new region, a wholesaler, an online channel. Volume rises with no change to the price.
**Change the product.** A smaller case for a market that cannot afford the large one, or a reformulation for buyers who had a reason not to buy.
**Promote it.** Advertising and in-store work reach buyers who had not considered the product rather than persuading existing ones to pay more.

body.text: Two of the four cost money up front and none of them is free. A wider distribution needs a discount to the wholesaler; a reformulation needs development; promotion is spent before any extra case is sold. So each route has to be judged against the extra revenue it brings, which is the comparison chapter 3 gives the tools for.

realExample.text: A drinks bottler that adds a small single-serve pack alongside its multipack reaches buyers who were never going to carry a multipack home. The product changed; the price per litre went up rather than down.

sections.misconception: Students answer every "improve sales" question with "advertise more". Name the route AND say who buys as a result: promotion reaches new buyers, distribution reaches new places, and a price cut reaches people for whom the old price was the obstacle.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Explain as requiring cause or effect supported by details or an example. "Advertise more" is not a cause; "advertise in the region the new depot serves, so the buyers who can now be supplied know the product exists" is.

sections.title: Ways of Improving Sales Revenues
sections.keyIdea: Revenue can be raised by a higher price or by more volume, and a price cut does both at once in opposite directions. Whether revenue rises depends on how much volume answers.

body.text: Revenue is price × volume, so there are two levers and they pull against each other. Raise the price and each case earns more while fewer are sold. Cut it and more are sold while each earns less.
Take the plant's cut from $6 to $5.40, which lifts volume from 20,000 to 24,000 cases. Revenue goes from $120,000 to $129,600 — up $9,600. The cut worked on revenue.

Now the other half. Those extra 4,000 cases carried $3.60 of variable cost each, so total cost went from $108,000 to $122,400. Profit is revenue less total cost: $129,600 − $122,400 = $7,200, against $12,000 before. **Revenue up $9,600, profit down $4,800.**

This is why the specification names volumes and revenues as two things, and why neither is the same as a third thing the firm actually wants. A route that improves revenue is worth having; it is not automatically worth taking.

realExample.text: A bottler that runs a promotional price for a quarter reports its best revenue quarter and a worse operating result than the quarter before it. Both figures are correct and they are measuring different things.

sections.misconception: Students assume higher revenue means higher profit, so "ways of improving sales revenues" becomes "ways of making more money". Revenue is one side of the calculation. The cases worth writing about are the ones where the two sides move opposite ways.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Analyse as requiring a brief chain of reasoning, and interpretation where it is applied to given data. The chain here has three links: lower price, higher volume, and the variable cost the higher volume brings with it.

recall.prompt: Try a different cut: $5.50 a case, selling 24,000. Work it per case:
template: Average cost at 24,000 cases is $___ a case
Revenue a case less average cost a case is $___
Multiply by 24,000 and profit ___ the $12,000 it was
hints: total cost over the output
the two per-case figures compared
which side of $12,000 the answer lands

takeaway: Sales revenue is price × volume, so the two can move opposite ways
A cost is fixed if output does not move it — for a stated period
Average cost falls because the fixed cost is spread wider
A price cut can raise revenue and lower profit at the same time

content.title: Sales Forecasting

sections.title: Purpose of Sales Forecasts
sections.keyIdea: A sales forecast is an estimate of future sales volume, and it is the first figure in the section: break-even, cash flow and every budget are built on top of it.

body.text: A **sales forecast** is an estimate of how much will be sold in a future period. It is a volume, usually by month, and it is the figure everything else in this section starts from.

Follow it through the plant. The forecast says 20,000 cases a month. That figure decides how much concentrate to order and how many shifts to roster; it is the output the break-even calculation is compared against; it is the receipts line of the cash-flow forecast; and it is the revenue line of the budget.

So the forecast is not a prediction the firm makes and files. It is a **planning figure**, and a wrong one is wrong four times over: too much concentrate, a margin of safety that was never there, a cash-flow forecast that promised receipts the firm will not get, and a budget every department is measured against.

That is also the honest answer to "how accurate does it need to be". Accurate enough that the decisions it drives would not have been different — which is a lower bar for a shift roster than for a decision to buy a second line.

realExample.text: A bottler orders concentrate three months ahead because the supplier ships by sea. The order is placed against a forecast, so the forecast is a commitment of cash long before any of it is sold.

sections.misconception: Students describe a forecast as a guess at next year's sales and stop. Say what it is FOR: every other figure in this topic is derived from it, which is why its difficulties matter more than its arithmetic.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Define as requiring the meaning of a term or phrase. Two marks for a sales forecast is the estimate and the period it covers, which are two things and not one said twice.

sections.title: Consumer Trends
sections.keyIdea: A consumer trend is a lasting change in what buyers want, and it moves a forecast because the past sales the forecast started from were made under the old preference.

body.text: The first of the specification's three factors. A **consumer trend** is a change in what buyers want that persists — not a good week, and not a seasonal swing that comes back the following year.

The plant's market is moving from sweetened drinks to lower-sugar ones. Half its range is sweetened, so the forecast for those lines is too high: last month's sales were made by buyers some of whom have now changed what they reach for. The adjustment is 2,000 cases off the base.

Direction is not the whole of it. A trend can also be an opportunity that a forecast built on the past cannot see: the low-sugar half of the same range is being carried by the same trend upwards, and a forecast that adjusts one line and not the other is wrong twice.
The hard part is telling a trend from a wobble, and the test is whether the reason for it is still true next year. A change in what people think a drink is for outlasts a hot month.

realExample.text: A bottler whose sweetened range had grown for a decade sees it flatten while its unsweetened line grows. Nothing about either product changed; what buyers wanted from the category did.

sections.misconception: Students use "consumer trends" as a label for anything to do with demand, including a competitor's price cut. A trend is a change in what buyers WANT. A rival's action is the third factor and is a change in what buyers are offered.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Analyse as requiring a brief chain of reasoning without evaluation. The chain is trend, then the product line it touches, then the direction the forecast moves — three links and no judgement at the end.

sections.title: Economic Variables
sections.keyIdea: Incomes, interest rates and exchange rates change how much buyers can spend and what the product costs them, so they move a forecast the firm has done nothing to cause.

body.text: The second factor. **Economic variables** are conditions outside the firm that change what buyers can spend or what the product costs them. Three matter for a forecast.

items: **Incomes.** Real incomes in the plant's region are rising, so a bottled drink is bought more often. The adjustment is +1,200 — 1,200 cases ONTO the base.
**Interest rates.** A rise leaves households with less after their borrowing is served, which shows up first in things bought casually rather than planned.
**Exchange rates.** The plant imports its concentrate, so a weaker local currency raises its costs, and a stronger one makes an imported rival cheaper on the shelf.

body.text: Notice that all three arrive as a change in VOLUME on the forecast even when they start as a change in a price or a cost. That is the discipline of this chapter: a forecast is a number of cases, so every factor has to be turned into cases before it can be used.
And the firm does not choose any of them. A forecast that ignores economic variables is not optimistic, it is incomplete.

realExample.text: A bottler importing concentrate and selling locally is exposed twice: a weaker local currency raises what it pays and leaves its buyers no better off. Neither effect is anything it did.

sections.misconception: Students write that a recession means lower sales for everyone. Say which variable and which direction for THIS product: a cheap everyday item can hold its volume in a downturn while a large pack does not.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Explain as requiring cause or effect supported by details. The detail that earns the second half is the route: rates to disposable income to this product's volume, not rates to "demand falls".

recall.prompt: A rise in the local currency makes the plant's imported concentrate cheaper and an imported rival cheaper too. Reason it through:
template: The plant's variable cost a case ___
Its contribution a case therefore ___
But the rival's shelf price ___ as well, so the forecast may still need cutting
hints: what a cheaper import does to the cost of a case
price less variable cost, with the price unmoved
the same exchange rate, on somebody else's costs

sections.title: Actions of Competitors
sections.keyIdea: A rival's price, product or distribution changes what the same buyers are offered, so a forecast built on the firm's own plans can be wrong without the firm changing anything.

body.text: The third factor, and the one a firm most often leaves out of its own forecast, because a forecast is usually built from the firm's plans and a competitor is not in them.
A rival is opening a plant in the plant's own region. It will compete for the same shelf space, and the adjustment is 3,000 cases off the base — the largest of the three.

A competitor can move a forecast four ways: a lower price, a new product, wider distribution, or promotion that reaches the same buyers first. The effect on the forecast is the same in kind each time — some of the volume the firm assumed was going to be sold by someone else.
The three factors together are why the revised figure is not simply the base one adjusted downwards. One of them adds and two subtract: 20,000 − 2,000 + 1,200 − 3,000 = 16,200 cases.

realExample.text: A regional bottler's volume falls the quarter a national brand starts delivering to the same wholesalers. Its own price, product and promotion were unchanged all quarter.

sections.misconception: Students treat a competitor's action as a consumer trend, because both end in lower sales. They are different factors with different answers: a trend is answered by changing the product, a competitor by changing the offer.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Analyse as including interpretation where it is applied to given data. Applied to a forecast table, that means saying which line moved and by how much, not that the forecast "may be inaccurate".

recall.prompt: All three factors are now taught. Match each change to which of them it is:

pairs.left: Households steadily switch to unsweetened drinks
pairs.why: A trend is a change in what buyers WANT, and it outlasts the year it starts in.

pairs.left: A rival wins the plant's largest wholesaler
pairs.why: A competitor changes what buyers are OFFERED, so the answer is to change the offer.

pairs.left: Interest rates rise and borrowing costs more
pairs.why: An economic variable changes what buyers can SPEND, and no firm chooses it.

pairs.left: A rival launches a pack the plant does not make
pairs.right: An action of a competitor, not a trend
pairs.why: Still the competitor factor, however much it looks like a change in taste.

sections.title: Difficulties of Sales Forecasting
sections.keyIdea: A forecast is hard because there may be no history to reason from, the three factors move together, the forecaster is not neutral, and better information costs money.

body.text: The specification asks for the difficulties in their own right, and they are not a list of ways the number can be wrong. They are reasons why it cannot be made much better.

items: **No history to forecast from.** A product the market has not seen has no past sales to reason from, so the forecast rests on judgement.
**The factors move together.** Incomes, tastes and a competitor can all change in one quarter, and their effects do not simply add.
**The forecaster is not neutral.** A forecast that has to justify a decision already taken is pulled towards the number that justifies it.
**Information costs money.** A better forecast needs research, and the research has to be worth less than the error it removes.

body.text: The third one is worth slowing down for, because it is the only one that is about a person. A forecast prepared to support a decision already taken is pulled towards the figure that supports it, and nobody in the process has to be dishonest for that to happen.
These four are also the limitations of everything built on the forecast. Chapter 4's receipts line and chapter 5's revenue budget are both this number, so both inherit all four.

realExample.text: A bottler launching an unfamiliar flavour has no past sales for it at all, so the forecast is built from a comparable product in another market and a judgement about how close the two are.

sections.misconception: Students answer this with "the forecast may be wrong", which is a restatement rather than a difficulty. Name the reason it is hard — no history, factors that interact, a forecaster with an interest, research that costs — and then say what that does to the decision.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Discuss as requiring chains of reasoning in context with a brief assessment showing awareness of competing factors. An eight-mark Discuss on forecasting needs two of these difficulties developed, not four named.

recall.prompt: Suppose the competitor's plant is delayed, so only the other two factors apply to the 20,000-case base:
template: The revised forecast would be ___ thousand cases
That is ___ thousand above the full three-factor figure
So the factor that moved the base furthest was the ___ one
hints: apply the trend and the income effect only
the size of the effect left out
which of the three was largest

takeaway: A forecast is a volume, and every other figure here is built on it
Three factors move it: consumer trends, economic variables, competitors
They do not all push the same way, so apply them one at a time
Its difficulties are inherited by the cash-flow forecast and the budget

content.title: Break-Even

sections.title: Contribution per Unit
sections.keyIdea: Contribution is selling price minus variable cost per unit. It is what one more unit leaves behind towards the fixed costs once its own costs are covered.

body.text: **Contribution = selling price − variable cost per unit.** For the plant: $6 − $3.60 = $2.40 a case.

The name says what it is for. Each case pays its own variable cost out of its own price, and what is left over CONTRIBUTES to the fixed costs. Sell one case and the plant is $2.40 nearer to covering the $36,000.
So contribution is not profit. Until the whole $36,000 has been covered there is no profit at all, however many cases have contributed. It is the rate at which the fixed cost is being paid off.

Because it is a per-case figure, only two things change it: the price and the variable cost per case. A change in the fixed costs leaves the contribution exactly where it was — which is why the three change cases later in this chapter behave differently from one another.

realExample.text: A bottler asked to quote for a one-off export order checks the contribution per case before the price: as long as the price covers the variable cost with something left over, the order helps pay costs the plant already owes.

sections.misconception: Students read contribution as profit per unit, so they multiply it out and call the answer profit. It is what is left towards the fixed costs. Nothing is profit until the fixed costs are covered.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Calculate as requiring workings shown. Contribution is a subtraction and the subtraction is the working: a bare $2.40 cannot be followed, because the marker cannot see which two figures produced it.

recall.prompt: The plant is asked to quote $4.90 a case on an export order. Its variable cost is unchanged:
template: Contribution on this order is ___ a case
That is ___ than the $2.40 on its usual price
Each case sold at $4.90 still leaves something towards the ___ costs
hints: price less the variable cost per case
compare the two contributions
what contribution contributes to

sections.title: The Break-Even Point
sections.keyIdea: The break-even point is the output at which total fixed costs plus total variable costs equal total revenue, so the firm makes neither a profit nor a loss.

body.text: The specification states it as an equality: **total fixed costs + total variable costs = total revenue.** The output at which that is true is the **break-even point**.

Check it on the plant at 15,000 cases. Revenue is $6 × 15,000 = $90,000. Costs are $36,000 + $3.60 × 15,000 = $36,000 + $54,000 = $90,000. The two are the same number, so the plant makes neither a profit nor a loss.
This is also the row flagged in chapter 1. Average cost at 15,000 cases is $90,000 ÷ 15,000 = $6, which is the selling price. A firm breaking even is one whose average cost has fallen to its price.

Neither a profit nor a loss is not the same as nothing happening. The $36,000 of fixed costs has been paid in full, and so has every $3.60 of variable cost. Break-even is the point at which the firm has covered everything it owes and no more.

realExample.text: A bottling plant commissioning a second line asks how many cases the line has to sell before it stops costing money. The answer is an output, not a date, and it is the same question as this one.

sections.misconception: Students describe break-even as the point where the firm "starts making money" and write it as a revenue. It is an OUTPUT — a number of units — at which two totals are equal. The revenue at that output is a different figure.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Define as requiring the meaning of a term. Break-even point defined without the words output or units has not said what kind of quantity it is.

sections.title: Using Contribution to Find the Break-Even Point
sections.keyIdea: The break-even point is fixed costs divided by contribution per unit, because contribution is the amount each unit pays towards the fixed costs.

body.text: Checking an output to see whether it breaks even is slow. The specification asks for the shortcut, and the shortcut is the contribution: **break-even point = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit.**
For the plant: $36,000 ÷ $2.40 = 15,000 cases. The same answer as the equality, in one step.

The division works because of what contribution is. Each case pays $2.40 towards the fixed costs, so the question "how many cases to cover $36,000" is a division and nothing more. If the formula is remembered without that sentence, it is remembered upside down as often as not.

And now the three cases the specification's interpretation bullet is really about. Change ONE figure at a time and the break-even point moves: price rises by $0.60 a case and it goes to 12,000; fixed costs rise by $6,000 a month and it goes to 17,500; variable cost rises by $0.40 a case and it goes to 18,000. A rise in fixed costs moves it by a different amount from a rise in variable cost, because the first changes the numerator and the second changes the divisor.

realExample.text: A bottler told its concentrate will cost more next year recalculates before it renegotiates: a rise in the variable cost per case raises the break-even point more than the same money added to the rent would.

sections.misconception: Students divide fixed costs by the selling price, or by the variable cost. The divisor is the CONTRIBUTION, because that is the part of the price that is available to pay the fixed costs at all.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Calculate as requiring a calculation based on given data with workings. A break-even answer needs the contribution line first: $6 − $3.60 = $2.40, then $36,000 ÷ $2.40.

recall.prompt: A fourth case: the plant renegotiates its rent and fixed costs FALL to $33,600 a month.
template: The break-even point becomes ___ thousand cases
It has moved ___
At 20,000 cases the margin of safety is now ___% of output
hints: the new fixed costs over the unchanged contribution
which way, against 15,000
the margin as a share of the output

sections.title: Margin of Safety
sections.keyIdea: The margin of safety is current or forecast output minus the break-even point: how far sales can fall, in units, before the firm stops covering its costs.

body.text: **Margin of safety = actual or forecast output − break-even point.** For the plant at 20,000 cases: 20,000 − 15,000 = 5,000 cases.

It is measured in cases, like the break-even point itself, and it answers one question: how much can go wrong before this stops working. 5,000 cases is 25% of the plant's output, so sales could fall by a quarter and it would still be covering its costs.

The figure is only as good as the output it starts from, which is why chapter 2 matters here. Apply the three forecast factors and output becomes 16,200 cases, so the margin of safety falls from 5,000 to 1,200 — from 25% of output to 7.4%. The break-even point never moved.

That is the useful shape of this idea. A margin of safety can shrink because the break-even point rose OR because the output fell, and the two have different answers: the first is a cost or price problem, the second is a demand problem.

realExample.text: A bottler with two thirds of its volume going to one wholesaler reads its margin of safety differently from one selling to thirty: the same number of cases is less reassuring when one customer can remove most of it.

sections.misconception: Students give the margin of safety as a money figure, usually the profit. It is a quantity of output. If a question asks for it in money, it wants the revenue or the profit at that output, and it will say so.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Calculate as requiring workings. A margin of safety answer shows the break-even point being worked out first, because the margin is a subtraction from it and cannot be checked without it.

sections.title: Interpreting a Break-Even Chart
sections.keyIdea: The revenue line starts at the origin and the cost line at the fixed costs. They cross at the break-even point, and the gap between them is the profit or the loss.

body.text: The specification asks for **interpretation** of break-even charts. Reading one is a matter of knowing where each line starts and what the space between them means.
**The revenue line starts at the origin.** Nothing sold is nothing earned, so at zero output revenue is zero. It rises by $6 for every case.

**The total cost line starts at the fixed costs.** At zero output the plant still owes $36,000, so the line begins at $36,000 on the money axis and rises by $3.60 a case — more gently than the revenue line, which is why they meet.

**They cross at the break-even point**, 15,000 cases and $90,000. Left of the crossing revenue is below costs and the vertical gap is a loss; right of it the gap is a profit. At 20,000 cases the gap is $120,000 − $108,000 = $12,000, which is the profit read straight off the chart.
The margin of safety is on the output axis, not in the money: the distance from 15,000 to 20,000. Two different questions, read in two different directions.

realExample.text: A lender reviewing a bottling plant's proposal looks first at how far the current output sits to the right of the crossing, because that distance is the room the plant has before the loan stops being serviced.

sections.misconception: Students draw the total cost line from the origin, which makes the fixed costs vanish and puts the crossing in the wrong place. The cost line starts at the fixed costs, because those are owed before a single unit is made.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Analyse as including interpretation when applied to given diagrams or data. Interpreting this chart means naming the output at the crossing and the gap at a stated output — reading values off it, not describing what the lines look like.

recall.prompt: On the plant's chart, sort each reading by where you look for it:

groups.name: Read on the output axis
items: The break-even point
The margin of safety
Output at the crossing
groups.why: Quantities of OUTPUT, so they are positions or distances along the horizontal axis.

groups.name: Read as a vertical gap
items: The profit at 20,000 cases
The loss at 10,000 cases
The fixed costs at zero output
groups.why: Amounts of MONEY, so they are heights or the gap between two heights.

sections.title: Limitations of Break-Even Analysis
sections.keyIdea: Break-even analysis assumes one price, a clean split between fixed and variable costs, and that everything made is sold — and it holds all three still.

body.text: The useful limitations are not "it might be wrong". They are the assumptions the straight lines are made of.

items: **One price for every case.** The chart draws revenue as a straight line, so it cannot show a discount for a large order.
**Costs split cleanly in two.** The split into fixed and variable is an assumption about the period, and a long enough period makes every cost variable.
**Everything made is sold.** Output and sales are the same axis on the chart, so unsold stock is invisible.
**A picture of one moment.** The chart holds price and costs still, and the three change cases show how far the point moves when they do not.

body.text: The second reaches furthest. Chapter 1 defined fixed and variable for a stated period, and over a long enough period every cost is a choice — so a break-even point worked out for a month cannot judge a three-year decision.
None of this makes the analysis useless. The three change cases are what it is good at. The limitation is in treating one point as a forecast rather than as a comparison.

realExample.text: A bottler that discounts heavily for large orders has no single selling price, so its revenue line is not straight and its chart puts the crossing further left than the discounted reality does.

sections.misconception: Students list limitations that are really forecasting difficulties — "the sales figures may be wrong". Those belong to chapter 2. A limitation of break-even analysis is something the METHOD assumes: one price, two kinds of cost, everything sold.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Evaluate as requiring a full awareness of the validity of competing factors leading to a conclusion that proposes a solution or recommendation. A twenty-mark answer here has to say what the firm should do given the limitation, not only that it exists.

recall.prompt: Put the steps of a break-even calculation in the order they have to be done:
items: Start from the selling price and the variable cost per case
Take one from the other to get the contribution per case
Divide the fixed costs by that contribution
Measure from the answer to current output for the margin of safety
correctOrder: Start from the selling price and the variable cost per case
Take one from the other to get the contribution per case
Divide the fixed costs by that contribution
Measure from the answer to current output for the margin of safety
why: Both are per-unit figures and nothing else can be worked out without them.
The contribution is the divisor, so it has to exist before the division.
This is the break-even point, and the margin of safety is measured from it.
The margin is a distance from the break-even point, so it can only come last.

takeaway: Contribution is price less variable cost per unit, not profit per unit
Break-even point = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit
Margin of safety is output less break-even, measured in units
The cost line starts at the fixed costs; the gap between lines is profit

content.title: Cash Flow

sections.title: Constructing a Cash-Flow Forecast
sections.keyIdea: A cash-flow forecast lists receipts and payments month by month. Net cash flow is receipts minus payments, and the closing balance is the opening balance plus that.

body.text: A **cash-flow forecast** is a table of money in and money out, month by month. Five lines, and they are always in the same order.

**Opening balance** is the cash the firm starts the month with. **Receipts** is money actually arriving. **Payments** is money actually leaving. **Net cash flow** is receipts − payments. **Closing balance** is opening balance + net cash flow — and it becomes the next month's opening balance, which is the line that makes the table a forecast rather than three separate months.

The word doing the work is ACTUALLY. The plant gives its customers 30 days to pay, so month 1's receipts are not month 1's sales — they are the 12,000 cases sold the month before, at $6, which is $72,000. Meanwhile month 1's payments are for month 1's output: $36,000 fixed plus $3.60 × 20,000 = $108,000.
Net cash flow for month 1 is therefore $72,000 − $108,000 = −$36,000, and a $30,000 opening balance closes at −$6,000. Nothing about the plant's trading went wrong in that month.

realExample.text: A bottler paying its concentrate supplier on delivery and collecting from wholesalers a month later carries the gap itself. The size of that gap is a line on the forecast, not an opinion about the customers.

sections.misconception: Students put sales on the receipts line in the month of the sale. A forecast is about when money moves, so a sale on credit appears in the month it is PAID. Getting this wrong shifts every closing balance after it.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Construct as requiring an accurately labelled diagram, and says the type may be stated or chosen. Constructing a cash-flow forecast means the five labelled lines in order, with the closing balance carried into the next column.

sections.title: Interpreting a Cash-Flow Forecast
sections.keyIdea: The line to read is the closing balance across the months: where it goes negative, and how deep, is the question the forecast was built to answer.

body.text: A constructed forecast is read along ONE line. The closing balance for the plant's three months runs −$6,000, then −$8,400, then $13,200.

Two things are worth saying about that sequence. It goes negative in month 1 and it is negative again in month 2, and the worst point is −$8,400. A negative closing balance means the plant needs cash it does not have — an overdraft, a delayed payment, or an owner putting money in.

And it recovers on its own by month 3, without the plant doing anything differently. $129,600 arrives — the month-2 sales being paid for — against $108,000 of payments, so the closing balance comes back to $13,200.

That shape is the whole argument for building the table. A shortfall that is visible three months ahead and known to be temporary is a conversation with a bank. The same shortfall discovered in the month it happens is an emergency, and it is the same $8,400.

realExample.text: A bottler's worst cash month is often the one after its best trading month, because the materials for the extra output were paid for before any of the extra sales were collected.

sections.misconception: Students read a negative closing balance as a loss. It is a shortage of cash. The trading in those months was unremarkable; what moved was the timing of the money.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Analyse as requiring a brief chain of reasoning and, applied to given data, interpretation. Interpreting this table means naming the month, the figure and the consequence — not that cash flow "could be a problem".

recall.prompt: Extend the forecast. Month 4 opens where month 3 closed, with receipts of $120,000 and payments of $108,000:
template: Net cash flow in month 4 is $___ thousand
The closing balance is $___ thousand
Four months in, the plant holds ___ than it started with
hints: receipts less payments for that month
month 3's closing balance plus it
compare it with $30,000

sections.title: Changing One Cash-Flow Variable
sections.keyIdea: Change one figure and every closing balance after it changes, because each month's closing balance is the next month's opening balance.

body.text: A forecast is most useful when it is asked a question. Change ONE variable, leave everything else alone, and read the closing balance line again.

Take the change from chapter 3: concentrate costs $0.40 more a case, so variable cost goes from $3.60 to $4. Payments rise in every month, by $0.40 times that month's output. Month 1's payments go from $108,000 to $116,000.

Now the closing balance line: −$14,000, then −$26,000, then −$12,400. All three are negative, the worst is −$26,000, and month 3 no longer recovers. The same $0.40 raised the break-even point from 15,000 to 18,000 cases in chapter 3.

One changed figure, read on two surfaces, answering two different questions: how much must we sell to cover our costs, and will we have the cash to get there. A firm needs both answers and neither one implies the other.

realExample.text: A bottler told its concentrate price will rise runs the new figure through both the break-even calculation and the cash-flow forecast before it replies, because the two answers can point to different decisions.

sections.misconception: Students change a figure in one month and leave the later months alone. The closing balance is carried forward, so a change in month 1 moves every month after it even if nothing else changes.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Calculate as requiring a calculation from given data with workings. A change case needs the changed line shown as well as the answer, because the marker has to see which variable moved.

sections.title: Use and Limitations of Cash-Flow Forecasts
sections.keyIdea: A forecast is used to arrange finance early, time the spending a firm controls and price its credit terms. Its limit is that every receipt on it is itself a forecast.

body.text: The specification pairs the uses with the limitations, and that is the point: the same table is valuable and unreliable for the same reason.
**What it is for.**

items: **Ask for finance early.** A shortfall shown three months ahead is a negotiation rather than an emergency.
**Time the spending you control.** An equipment payment can move to a month with a receipt in it; a wage bill cannot.
**Price the terms you offer.** The table says what thirty days of credit costs, which makes it a decision.

body.text: **What it cannot do.**

items: **The receipts are forecasts.** Each one is a sales forecast, so chapter 2's difficulties are in this table.
**A customer can pay late.** One large customer taking sixty days moves every balance after it.
**It says nothing about why.** It shows a shortfall and not its cause, so it starts the investigation.

body.text: The first limitation connects this chapter to chapter 2: every figure on the receipts line is a sales forecast, so all four difficulties are in this table too — and compounded, because a forecast wrong about the amount is usually wrong about the timing.

realExample.text: A lender asked for an overdraft three months before it is needed is being shown a plan. The same lender asked in the week the balance turns negative is being asked to rescue something.

sections.misconception: Students treat a cash-flow forecast as a record of what happened. It is a forecast, and its receipts line is built on the sales forecast from chapter 2 — so it inherits every difficulty that number has.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Assess as requiring a balanced and wide-ranging assessment showing awareness of competing factors, leading to a supported judgement. A ten-mark Assess of a forecast needs a use and a limitation, and then a view on which matters more for this firm.

recall.prompt: Order what the plant does with the forecast, from building it to acting on it:
items: Forecast the sales volume for each month
Turn the sales into receipts using the credit terms
Set the payments against each month's output
Carry the closing balance into the next month
Arrange finance for the month the balance turns negative
correctOrder: Forecast the sales volume for each month
Turn the sales into receipts using the credit terms
Set the payments against each month's output
Carry the closing balance into the next month
Arrange finance for the month the balance turns negative
why: Nothing on the table can be filled in before the volume is estimated.
A sale becomes a receipt only when it is paid, so the credit terms decide the month.
Payments follow what is PRODUCED, which is not what is collected.
This is the step that makes three separate months into one forecast.
The action comes last, and it is the reason for building the table at all.

takeaway: Receipts are money arriving, not sales made — credit terms decide when
Closing balance is opening plus net cash flow, carried into next month
Change one variable and every month after it changes
Its receipts line is a sales forecast, so it inherits those difficulties

content.title: Budgets

sections.title: Purposes of Budgets
sections.keyIdea: A budget is an agreed plan in figures for a future period. It is used to plan, to control spending as it happens, to motivate whoever agreed it, and to allocate a fixed total.

body.text: A **budget** is a financial plan for a future period, agreed in advance. The plant's Month 2 budget says revenue $120,000, variable costs $72,000, fixed costs $36,000.
It does four jobs, and they are genuinely different jobs.

items: **Plan.** A budget turns a target into figures a department can be given.
**Control.** Spending can be compared with the figure agreed, monthly, while there is time to act.
**Motivate.** A figure somebody accepted is a target they own, which an instruction is not.
**Allocate.** A fixed total forces a choice between the departments asking for it.

body.text: Control is the one that makes a budget worth the work. A set of annual accounts tells a firm what happened after it can do anything about it; a monthly budget compared with the actual figures tells it in time to act, which is what chapter 5's variance analysis is for.
And the fourth job is the one students leave out. When the total is fixed, giving one department more means giving another less, so a budget forces a choice that would otherwise be avoided.

realExample.text: A bottling plant's maintenance and marketing managers both want the same unallocated sum. The budget is where that is settled, and it is settled once rather than argued about monthly.

sections.misconception: Students describe a budget as a limit on spending. It is a plan, and a plan for revenue as much as for costs — a sales budget is a target to reach, not a ceiling to stay under.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Explain as requiring cause or effect with details or an example. A purpose explained needs the mechanism: control works because the comparison happens monthly, while there is still time to change something.

sections.title: Budgets Based on Historical Figures
sections.keyIdea: A historical budget starts from last period's actual figures and adjusts them. It is quick and it carries forward whatever was in last period's spending, justified or not.

body.text: The specification names two types of budget. The first starts from what happened: last period's actual figures, adjusted for what is expected to change. The plant's $36,000 fixed-cost budget is last month's figure with an expected rent increase in it.

**Why firms use it.** It is fast, the figures already exist, and it is easy to explain to whoever has to accept it. For a cost that genuinely does not move much, starting from last month is not lazy — it is correct.

**What it carries forward.** Everything in last period's spending comes with it, including the part nobody could now justify. A line that was set for a product the plant no longer makes is adjusted by the same percentage as the rest, year after year, because nobody is ever asked what it is for.

So the weakness is not inaccuracy. A historical budget is usually close to right. It is that the method never asks whether the base it starts from deserved to be there, which is exactly the question the second type is built around.

realExample.text: A plant's stationery and subscriptions line rises by the same few per cent every year and nobody in the building can say what is on it. That is a historical budget working exactly as designed.

sections.misconception: Students say a historical budget "uses old data and is therefore wrong". It is usually close. The objection is that it never tests the base — a figure can be accurate and unjustified at the same time.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Assess as requiring a balanced assessment leading to a supported judgement. Assessing a budgeting method means the case for the speed as well as the case against the inherited base, then a view for this firm.

sections.title: Zero-Based Budgets
sections.keyIdea: A zero-based budget starts every line at nothing and each one has to be justified from scratch. It tests what a historical budget assumes, and it costs a great deal of time.

body.text: The second type. The specification calls it **zero based**, and the name is literal: every line starts at nothing and every amount asked for has to be justified from the beginning, whatever it was last period.

**What it finds.** Spending that survived because nobody questioned it. If the plant's marketing manager has to argue for the whole figure rather than for the increase, the parts that cannot be argued for do not get funded. That is the one thing a historical budget can never do.

**What it costs.** Time, and a lot of it. Every line means a case prepared, a meeting and a decision, across every department, for a budget that may be very close to last year's anyway. A firm that did this monthly would do little else.

Which is why the real choice is not one method or the other. A firm can budget historically as a rule and take one area to zero base each year — the speed where the base is sound, the scrutiny where it is doubtful.

realExample.text: A plant that zero bases its maintenance budget once discovers a service contract for equipment that was sold two years earlier. The historical method had been adjusting that line upwards the whole time.

sections.misconception: Students write that zero-based budgeting "sets the budget to zero". It sets the STARTING POINT to zero: the department still gets a budget, but it gets one it has argued for rather than one it inherited.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Evaluate as requiring a perceptive conclusion that proposes a solution or recommendation. The recommendation here is rarely one method for everything, and a conclusion that picks one without saying where it applies has not weighed the cost.

recall.prompt: Match each budgeting problem to the method that answers it:

pairs.left: A spending line nobody can justify
pairs.why: Starting from zero forces the case to be made rather than inherited.

pairs.left: A budget needed quickly, for a stable cost
pairs.why: The figures already exist, and a stable cost does not need re-arguing.

pairs.left: Managers who will not accept the target
pairs.why: A figure somebody agreed to is a target they own; an imposed one is not.
The monthly comparison catches drift while there is still time to act.

sections.title: Variance Analysis
sections.keyIdea: A variance is the difference between a budgeted figure and the actual one: favourable when it helps profit, adverse when it hurts it. None means anything alone.

body.text: A **variance** is the difference between what was budgeted and what happened. It is called **favourable** when it helps profit and **adverse** when it hurts profit — which means the same arithmetic reads opposite ways on a revenue line and a cost line.
Revenue above budget is favourable. Cost above budget is adverse. So a variance is never just a number: it is a number and a word, and getting the word wrong inverts the meaning.

The plant's Month 2: revenue was budgeted at $120,000 and came in at $129,600, a variance of $9,600 **favourable**. Variable costs were budgeted at $72,000 and came in at $86,400 — $14,400 **adverse**. Fixed costs were $2,400 **adverse**.
Now add them up the way they affect profit: $9,600 favourable less $14,400 and $2,400 adverse is $7,200 **adverse** — and the profit variance is exactly that. Budgeted $12,000, actual $4,800.

**The best revenue month was the worse profit month.** The extra cases were sold at a lower price and they carried their variable costs with them, which is the price cut from chapter 1 arriving on the budget. A favourable variance on one line is not good news until the other lines have been read.

realExample.text: A bottler celebrating a record sales month finds the same month's profit below budget. Both reports are right, and the variance table is the only place the two are reconciled.

sections.misconception: Students read favourable as good and adverse as bad, and stop. A favourable sales variance won by discounting brings an adverse cost variance with it. Read the lines together and check that they reconcile to the profit variance.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Analyse as requiring a brief chain of reasoning and, on given data, interpretation. Interpreting a variance table means linking the lines — this favourable one caused that adverse one — rather than describing each in turn.

recall.prompt: Suppose the fixed costs had come in at $34,800 instead of $38,400, with the other two lines unchanged:
template: The fixed-cost variance would be $___ thousand
and it would be ___
Profit would still miss its budget, by $___ thousand
hints: the difference from the budgeted figure
which way it moves profit
net the three variances against each other

sections.title: Difficulties of Budgeting
sections.keyIdea: A budget is built on a sales forecast, it rewards spending the whole allowance, it demotivates when the target is set too high, and it takes real time to negotiate.

body.text: The difficulties of budgeting are a leaf in their own right, and not the same as the drawbacks of one method.

items: **It is built on a forecast.** A budget starts from a sales forecast and inherits chapter 2's difficulties.
**Spending to protect the allowance.** A department that underspends can expect less next year.
**A target set too high demotivates.** A figure nobody believes is a figure nobody works towards.
**It takes time to set.** The meetings and the negotiation are a real cost, felt most by a small firm.

body.text: The first closes the loop this section opened. A variance measured against a forecast that was wrong tells the firm about its forecasting, not about its performance.

The second, firms create for themselves. If underspending means a smaller allowance next year, the rational thing to do in month twelve is spend the balance — so a rule meant to control spending has produced some.
None of these is a reason not to budget. They are reasons to read a variance as the start of a question, which is where this section began: every figure in it rests on the one before.

realExample.text: A department that comes in under budget two years running finds its allowance cut, and spends to the limit in the third. Nothing in the process was dishonest and the incentive was doing exactly what it was set up to do.

sections.misconception: Students give "the budget might be wrong" as a difficulty. Say why it is hard to get right — it inherits the sales forecast, it changes how people behave, and it costs time — and then what the firm should do about it.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Discuss as requiring logical chains of reasoning in context with a brief assessment showing awareness of competing arguments. Two difficulties developed with what the firm should do beats four listed.

takeaway: A budget plans, controls, motivates and allocates a fixed total
Historical is fast and inherits its base; zero based tests it and costs time
A variance is a number and a word: favourable or adverse
Variances reconcile to the profit variance — read them together

notes.title: Sales, Revenue and Costs
notes.content:
**Sales Volume and Sales Revenue.** Sales volume is how many units are sold; sales revenue is what they were sold for. Revenue is price multiplied by volume, so the two can move in opposite directions.

**Fixed and Variable Costs.** A fixed cost does not change when output changes; a variable cost does. The split is a statement about a period of time, not about the kind of cost.

**Total Costs and Average Costs.** Total cost is fixed plus variable at that output. Average cost is total cost divided by output, and it falls as output rises because the fixed cost is spread wider.

**Ways of Improving Sales Volumes.** Volume is raised by giving more buyers a reason to buy: a lower price, a wider distribution, a change to the product, or promotion that reaches people who had not considered it.

**Ways of Improving Sales Revenues.** Revenue can be raised by a higher price or by more volume, and a price cut does both at once in opposite directions. Whether revenue rises depends on how much volume answers.

notes.title: Sales Forecasting
notes.content:
**Purpose of Sales Forecasts.** A sales forecast is an estimate of future sales volume, and it is the first figure in the section: break-even, cash flow and every budget are built on top of it.

**Consumer Trends.** A consumer trend is a lasting change in what buyers want, and it moves a forecast because the past sales the forecast started from were made under the old preference.

**Economic Variables.** Incomes, interest rates and exchange rates change how much buyers can spend and what the product costs them, so they move a forecast the firm has done nothing to cause.

**Actions of Competitors.** A rival's price, product or distribution changes what the same buyers are offered, so a forecast built on the firm's own plans can be wrong without the firm changing anything.

**Difficulties of Sales Forecasting.** A forecast is hard because there may be no history to reason from, the three factors move together, the forecaster is not neutral, and better information costs money.

notes.title: Break-Even
notes.content:
**Contribution per Unit.** Contribution is selling price minus variable cost per unit. It is what one more unit leaves behind towards the fixed costs once its own costs are covered.

**The Break-Even Point.** The break-even point is the output at which total fixed costs plus total variable costs equal total revenue, so the firm makes neither a profit nor a loss.

**Using Contribution to Find the Break-Even Point.** The break-even point is fixed costs divided by contribution per unit, because contribution is the amount each unit pays towards the fixed costs.

**Margin of Safety.** The margin of safety is current or forecast output minus the break-even point: how far sales can fall, in units, before the firm stops covering its costs.

**Interpreting a Break-Even Chart.** The revenue line starts at the origin and the cost line at the fixed costs. They cross at the break-even point, and the gap between them is the profit or the loss.

**Limitations of Break-Even Analysis.** Break-even analysis assumes one price, a clean split between fixed and variable costs, and that everything made is sold — and it holds all three still.

notes.title: Cash Flow
notes.content:
**Constructing a Cash-Flow Forecast.** A cash-flow forecast lists receipts and payments month by month. Net cash flow is receipts minus payments, and the closing balance is the opening balance plus that.

**Interpreting a Cash-Flow Forecast.** The line to read is the closing balance across the months: where it goes negative, and how deep, is the question the forecast was built to answer.

**Changing One Cash-Flow Variable.** Change one figure and every closing balance after it changes, because each month's closing balance is the next month's opening balance.

**Use and Limitations of Cash-Flow Forecasts.** A forecast is used to arrange finance early, time the spending a firm controls and price its credit terms. Its limit is that every receipt on it is itself a forecast.

notes.title: Budgets
notes.content:
**Purposes of Budgets.** A budget is an agreed plan in figures for a future period. It is used to plan, to control spending as it happens, to motivate whoever agreed it, and to allocate a fixed total.

**Budgets Based on Historical Figures.** A historical budget starts from last period's actual figures and adjusts them. It is quick and it carries forward whatever was in last period's spending, justified or not.

**Zero-Based Budgets.** A zero-based budget starts every line at nothing and each one has to be justified from scratch. It tests what a historical budget assumes, and it costs a great deal of time.

**Variance Analysis.** A variance is the difference between a budgeted figure and the actual one: favourable when it helps profit, adverse when it hurts it. None means anything alone.

**Difficulties of Budgeting.** A budget is built on a sales forecast, it rewards spending the whole allowance, it demotivates when the target is set too high, and it takes real time to negotiate.

quiz.question: Sales revenue is calculated as:
options: selling price minus variable cost per unit
total cost divided by output
sales volume minus the break-even point
selling price multiplied by sales volume
quiz.explanation: Revenue is money, and it is the product of the two figures the specification names separately: the price each unit sold for and how many were sold. Price minus variable cost per unit is contribution, and total cost divided by output is average cost — both are per-unit figures, not a total.

quiz.question: For one month at a bottling plant, which of these is a fixed cost?
options: the concentrate used in each case
the insurance premium on the factory
the bottles and caps
the electricity used while the line runs
quiz.explanation: The test is whether OUTPUT moves the cost. An insurance premium agreed for the month is owed whether the line bottles nothing or runs flat out. Concentrate, packaging and the power drawn by a running line all rise case by case, so all three vary with output.

quiz.question: Average cost falls as output rises mainly because:
options: the fixed costs are spread over more units
the variable cost per unit falls as more are made
the selling price rises with output
total cost stops rising once output is high enough
quiz.explanation: Only the fixed half is being divided by a bigger number; the variable cost per unit is the same at every output, which is what makes it variable. Total cost keeps rising as long as anything is being made, and the selling price is a decision rather than a function of output.

quiz.question: A plant sells 18,000 cases at $6.50 each. Its sales revenue is:
quiz.explanation: Revenue is $6.50 × 18,000 = $117,000. $108,000 is 18,000 at the plant's usual $6, and $120,000 is 20,000 at $6 — both are revenue figures for a different price or a different volume.

quiz.question: Fixed costs are $36,000 a month and variable cost is $3.60 a case. Total cost at 20,000 cases is:
quiz.explanation: Total cost is the fixed costs plus the total variable cost: $36,000 + $3.60 × 20,000 = $36,000 + $72,000 = $108,000. $72,000 leaves the fixed costs out altogether, and $36003.60 adds one case's variable cost instead of 20,000 cases'.

quiz.question: With the same costs, average cost at 25,000 cases is:
quiz.explanation: Average cost is total cost divided by output: $126,000 ÷ 25,000 = $5.04. $3.60 is the variable cost per case and leaves the fixed costs out; $1.44 is the fixed cost per case and leaves the variable costs out; $5.40 is the average cost at 20,000 cases.

quiz.question: A plant cuts its price from $6 to $5.40 and sales rise from 20,000 to 24,000 cases. Which is true?
options: revenue and profit both rise
revenue and profit both fall
revenue rises and profit falls
revenue falls and profit rises
quiz.explanation: Revenue goes from $120,000 to $129,600, up $9,600. Profit goes from $12,000 to $7,200, because the extra 4,000 cases each carried $3.60 of variable cost. The two sides of the calculation move opposite ways, which is why the specification names volume and revenue separately.

quiz.question: Which of these raises sales VOLUME without changing the price?
options: reducing the price to match the cheapest rival
raising the price to signal a better product
offering a discount on orders above a hundred cases
supplying a wholesaler in a region the plant does not yet reach
quiz.explanation: Widening distribution puts the same product at the same price in front of buyers who could not get it before. Matching a rival's price and discounting large orders are both price changes, and raising the price is a price change in the other direction.

quiz.question: A sales forecast is best described as:
options: a record of what was sold in the last period
a target the sales team is contractually committed to
the output at which a firm covers all of its costs
an estimate of sales volume for a future period
quiz.explanation: A forecast is forward-looking and it is a volume. A record of the last period is where a forecast often starts, but it is not the forecast. The output at which all costs are covered is the break-even point, which is a different calculation on a different chapter.

quiz.question: Which of these is a consumer trend rather than an action of a competitor?
options: a rival cutting its wholesale price for six months
a rival winning a listing with the plant's largest customer
a rival launching a single-serve pack
buyers steadily moving from sweetened drinks to lower-sugar ones
quiz.explanation: A consumer trend is a lasting change in what buyers WANT. The other three are all changes in what buyers are OFFERED, which is the third factor — and the specification lists them separately because they have different answers.

quiz.question: Rising real incomes in a plant's region would be expected to:
options: lower the forecast, because buyers trade up to other categories
leave the forecast unchanged, since incomes are outside the firm
lower the forecast, because costs rise with incomes
raise the forecast, because a casual purchase is made more often
quiz.explanation: More to spend means a low-cost everyday item is bought more often, so the forecast rises. A factor being outside the firm's control is a reason to include it rather than a reason to ignore it, and the effect on the firm's own wage costs is a separate question from the volume it will sell.

quiz.question: A base forecast of 20,000 cases is adjusted by 2,000 down for consumer trends, 1,200 up for economic variables and 3,000 down for a new competitor. The revised forecast is:
options: 15,000 cases
19,200 cases
16,200 cases
21,200 cases
quiz.explanation: All three adjustments apply: 20,000 − 2,000 + 1,200 − 3,000 = 16,200. Each of the other three figures leaves one factor out — the rise, the competitor, or both falls — and the first of those is the commonest error here, because the factors do not all point the same way.

quiz.question: A plant is forecasting sales of a product it has never sold. Its central problem is that:
options: a forecast has to be expressed as a volume
there are no past sales of it to reason from
forecasts are prepared before the period they cover
the sales team rather than the finance team prepares it
quiz.explanation: No history is the difficulty the specification's own leaf points at, and it is why a launch forecast rests on judgement about a comparable product. Being expressed as a volume and being prepared in advance are simply what a forecast IS, and who prepares it matters only through the interest they have in the answer.

quiz.question: Selling price is $6 and variable cost is $3.60 a case. Contribution per case is:
quiz.explanation: Contribution is selling price minus variable cost per unit: $6 − $3.60 = $2.40. It is what each case leaves towards the fixed costs once its own variable cost is covered, so it is neither the price nor the cost nor the two added together.

quiz.question: Fixed costs are $36,000 and contribution is $2.40 a case. The break-even point is:
options: 15,000 cases
6,000 cases
10,000 cases
quiz.explanation: The break-even point is fixed costs divided by contribution per unit: $36,000 ÷ $2.40 = 15,000 cases. 6,000 divides by the selling price and 10,000 by the variable cost — neither is the part of the price available to pay the fixed costs. $90,000 is the revenue AT break-even, which is money rather than output.

quiz.question: The plant breaks even at 15,000 cases and currently makes 20,000. Its margin of safety is:
options: 20,000 cases
5,000 cases
quiz.explanation: Margin of safety is output minus the break-even point, in units: 20,000 − 15,000 = 5,000 cases. $12,000 is the profit at that output, which is a money figure; 75% is the break-even point as a share of output, which is the margin looked at from the wrong end.

quiz.question: The plant's rent goes up, adding $6,000 a month to its overheads. Nothing else moves. What happens?
options: rises to 18,000 cases
rises to 17,500 cases
falls to 12,000 cases
stays at 15,000 cases, since contribution is unchanged
quiz.explanation: A rise in fixed costs changes the numerator: $42,000 ÷ $2.40 = 17,500 cases. Contribution IS unchanged, which is exactly why the division still works — but the amount to be covered is larger, so more cases are needed. 18,000 is what a $0.40 rise in variable cost would give, which moves the divisor instead.

quiz.question: On a break-even chart, the total cost line:
options: starts at the level of the fixed costs
starts at the origin, like the revenue line
is horizontal across every output
crosses the revenue line at the margin of safety
quiz.explanation: At zero output the firm still owes its fixed costs, so the total cost line begins at that height and rises by the variable cost per unit. A line from the origin would make the fixed costs vanish; the horizontal line is the FIXED cost line; and the point where the two cross is the break-even point, with the margin of safety measured along the output axis from there.

quiz.question: A plant gives 30 days' credit. Month 1's receipts on its cash-flow forecast are:
options: month 1's sales, whether or not they have been paid for
month 1's sales plus the opening balance
the profit earned in month 1
the previous month's sales, collected in month 1
quiz.explanation: A cash-flow forecast records money moving, so a sale on credit appears in the month it is PAID. Putting month 1's own sales on the receipts line is the commonest error and it shifts every closing balance after it. The opening balance is its own line, and profit does not appear on the forecast at all.

quiz.question: How is the figure at the foot of each month's column worked out?
options: receipts minus payments for that month
the opening balance plus net cash flow
the opening balance plus receipts
total receipts for the whole forecast period
quiz.explanation: The closing balance is what the firm starts with plus what the month added or took away, and it becomes next month's opening balance. Receipts minus payments is the NET CASH FLOW, which is one of the two numbers that make up the closing balance rather than the balance itself.

quiz.question: Month 2 opens at −$6,000, with receipts of $120,000 and payments of $122,400. The closing balance is:
quiz.explanation: Net cash flow is $120,000 − $122,400 = −$2,400, and the closing balance is −$6,000 + −$2,400 = −$8,400. Stopping at −$2,400 leaves out the balance carried in, and treating a negative opening balance as a positive one moves the answer the wrong way by twice its size.

quiz.question: A negative closing balance on a cash-flow forecast means the firm:
options: has made a trading loss in that month
has sold less than its break-even point that month
has overestimated the fixed costs in its budget
will be short of cash that month unless it arranges some
quiz.explanation: A negative closing balance is a shortage of CASH: the money leaving that month exceeds the money arriving plus what was in hand. The month's trading can be perfectly profitable — the plant's is — because what moved was the timing of the money rather than the margin on it.

quiz.question: Which of these is a limitation of a cash-flow forecast?
options: every figure on the receipts line is itself a sales forecast
it shows the timing of payments rather than their size
it cannot be prepared for more than one month at a time
it records only cash and not payments made by transfer
quiz.explanation: The receipts line inherits the sales forecast and therefore every difficulty of forecasting. A forecast shows timing AND size, is normally prepared for six or twelve months, and "cash" here means money moving by any route, not notes and coins.

quiz.question: Which of these is a purpose of a budget?
options: to record what each department spent last year
to set a ceiling that no department may exceed for any reason
to allocate a fixed total between departments that both want it
to replace the need for a sales forecast
quiz.explanation: When the total is fixed, giving one department more means giving another less, so the budget is where that choice gets settled. Recording last year's spending is where a historical budget STARTS; a budget is a plan for revenue as well as for costs rather than a ceiling; and its revenue line is a sales forecast, so it depends on one.

quiz.question: The difference between a zero-based budget and one based on historical figures is that a zero-based budget:
options: sets every department's budget to nothing
is prepared by the finance team rather than the department
requires every amount to be justified from the beginning
is used only by firms that made a loss last year
quiz.explanation: Zero based means the STARTING POINT is zero: the department still receives a budget, but one it has argued for rather than inherited. That is why it finds spending a historical budget carries forward unexamined, and why it costs so much more time to prepare.

quiz.question: Variable costs were budgeted at $72,000 and came in at $86,400. The variance is:
options: $14,400 adverse
$14,400 favourable
$9,600 adverse
$86,400 adverse
quiz.explanation: The difference is $14,400, and on a cost line spending above budget reduces profit, so it is adverse. $9,600 is the revenue variance for the same month, which is favourable — the same arithmetic reads opposite ways on a revenue line and a cost line.

quiz.question: In one month a plant's sales revenue beat its budget by $9,600 and its profit missed by $7,200. The best explanation is that:
options: the revenue variance must have been recorded with the wrong sign
the extra sales were made at a lower price and carried variable costs with them
fixed costs must have risen by more than the revenue variance
a favourable revenue variance has no effect on profit
quiz.explanation: The extra cases were sold at $5.40 rather than $6 and each one added $3.60 of variable cost, so $9,600 favourable less $14,400 and $2,400 adverse is $7,200 adverse. The fixed-cost variance was only $2,400, and a revenue variance certainly affects profit — it is simply not the only line that does.

quiz.question: Which of these is a difficulty of budgeting?
options: a budget is set for a whole year and never for a month
underspending is punished with a smaller allowance the following year
a budget removes the need to compare actual figures with plan
variances are calculated after the year has ended, too late to act
quiz.explanation: If underspending is punished with a smaller allowance, the rational thing to do at the end of the period is spend the balance — so a rule meant to control spending has produced some. Budgets are normally set monthly as well as annually, and the monthly comparison of actual against plan is the whole point of having one.

practice.question: Define the term 'margin of safety'. (2 marks)
practice.guidance:
Two marks means two separate things to say and the second is not a rewording of the first. Before you write, settle what KIND of quantity this is — the commonest loss of a mark here is answering in money when the term is measured in something else.
The margin of safety is the difference between a firm's current or forecast output and its break-even point (1 mark), measured in units of output, and it shows how far sales could fall before the firm stopped covering its costs (1 mark). For the plant, 20,000 − 15,000 = 5,000 cases. An answer giving a money figure has described the profit at that output instead, which is a different quantity.

practice.question: A bottling plant has fixed costs of $36,000 a month and a variable cost of $3.60 a case. Calculate its total cost and its average cost at an output of 25,000 cases. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
Two figures are wanted and the second is built out of the first, so do them in order and label both. Appendix 6 says a Calculate requires workings to be shown, and here the workings are where the marks are — decide which total you need before you divide anything.
Total variable cost is $3.60 × 25,000 = $90,000 (1 mark). Total cost is $36,000 + $90,000 = $126,000 (1 mark). Average cost is total cost divided by output: $126,000 ÷ 25,000 (1 mark) = $5.04 a case (1 mark). Dividing only the fixed costs gives $1.44 and dividing only the variable costs gives $3.60; both leave half the total out.

practice.question: A bottling plant is launching a flavour that has never been sold in its region. Explain one difficulty it will face in forecasting sales of the new flavour. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
One difficulty, explained — not a list. Appendix 6 defines Explain as requiring a brief explanation of cause or effect supported by details or an example, so the shape is a named difficulty, the reason it arises HERE, and what it does to the forecast. Choose the difficulty that the words "never been sold in its region" are pointing at.
The difficulty is that there are no past sales of this flavour to reason from (1 mark), because the region has never been offered it, so the usual starting point for a forecast does not exist (1 mark). The plant must instead build the forecast from a comparable product — the same flavour in another market, or a similar flavour in this one — and a judgement about how close the comparison is (1 mark). That judgement can be wrong in either direction, so the forecast has a much wider range of error than one for an established line, and every figure built on it (the cash-flow forecast, the budget) inherits that range (1 mark). An answer that says only "the forecast may be inaccurate" has named no cause.

practice.question: A bottling plant sells at $6 a case with a variable cost of $3.60 a case and fixed costs of $36,000 a month. Calculate its break-even point, and calculate the new break-even point if the variable cost rises to $4. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
Two break-even points, and the second is the first done again with one figure changed. Appendix 6 requires workings, and on this question the working that matters is the line before the division — get that wrong and both answers are wrong together. Note which of the three given figures actually moves.
Contribution is $6 − $3.60 = $2.40 (1 mark), so the break-even point is $36,000 ÷ $2.40 = 15,000 cases (1 mark).
