With variable cost at $4, contribution falls to $2 (1 mark) and the break-even point becomes $36,000 ÷ $2 = 18,000 cases (1 mark). The fixed costs never changed, so an answer that adjusts them has moved the wrong figure; dividing by the price rather than the contribution gives 6,000 and misses what contribution is for.

practice.question: A plant opens month 1 with $30,000. It expects receipts of $72,000, $120,000 and $129,600 and payments of $108,000, $122,400 and $108,000 over three months. Construct a cash-flow forecast showing net cash flow and the closing balance for each month. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 defines Construct as requiring an accurately labelled diagram, so the labels are part of what is being asked rather than decoration on top of it. Set the table out before you calculate anything: decide your five row labels and your three column headings first, and be clear which row feeds the next month.
Five labelled rows — opening balance, receipts, payments, net cash flow, closing balance — across three labelled months (1 mark). Net cash flow is receipts less payments each month: −$36,000, −$2,400, $21,600 (1 mark). Closing balance is opening plus net cash flow: $30,000 + −$36,000 = −$6,000 (1 mark). Each closing balance is carried down as the next month's opening balance, giving −$6,000 then −$8,400 then $13,200 (1 mark). A table whose three months each open at $30,000 has missed the line that makes it one forecast rather than three.

practice.question: A bottling plant budgets historically: each line is last year's actual figure adjusted for expected changes. Its finance manager has found a service contract for equipment sold two years ago, and proposes moving the whole firm to zero-based budgeting from next year. Assess whether the plant should do so. (10 marks)
practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 defines Assess as requiring a coherent and logical chain of reasoning, well contextualised, with a balanced and wide-ranging assessment showing awareness of competing factors and leading to a supported judgement. Plan the judgement before you write the case, so the two sides you develop are the two the judgement actually turns on. The words "the whole firm" in the last sentence are doing work.
The case for: zero-based budgeting starts every line at nothing and requires each amount to be justified, which is the only method that tests the base a historical budget carries forward. The plant has direct evidence of the problem — a service contract on equipment it no longer owns, which has been adjusted upwards annually because nobody was ever asked what it was for. Scrutiny of that kind also changes behaviour: a manager who expects to argue for the whole figure prepares differently from one who expects to argue for the increase.
The case against: the cost is time, and it scales with the number of lines. Every line means a case prepared, a meeting and a decision, across every department, to arrive at figures that for stable costs will be close to last year's anyway — the rent and the insurance do not become better understood by being re-argued. There is also a risk in the transition year, when managers are learning a new process and the budget still has to be set on time.
The judgement most defensible on this evidence is that the plant should NOT move the whole firm at once. The problem it found is a problem of unexamined lines, not of every line, so the proportionate answer is to budget historically as a rule and zero base one area each year, starting with the one the service contract was in. That gets the scrutiny where the evidence points it and keeps the speed where the base is sound. A judgement that simply picks one method for everything has not weighed the cost of the scrutiny against the value of it.

practice.question: A bottling plant sells at $6 a case, with a variable cost of $3.60 and fixed costs of $36,000 a month. It breaks even at 15,000 cases and currently produces 20,000. Its owner discounts heavily on orders above a hundred cases and is considering a second production line. Evaluate the usefulness of break-even analysis to the owner in making that decision. (20 marks)
practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 defines Evaluate as requiring fully developed, coherent and logical chains of reasoning, a full awareness of the validity and significance of competing factors, and a perceptive conclusion that proposes a solution or recommendation. So the conclusion has to tell the owner what to DO, not only how useful the technique is. Two details in the stem are there to be used against the analysis — find them before you plan.
Where it is useful: break-even analysis gives the owner a figure the decision can be tested against. A second line raises fixed costs, and the analysis says immediately what that does — the break-even point rises in proportion, so the owner can ask whether the extra output can actually be sold. It also quantifies the room for error: a margin of safety of 5,000 cases, 25% of current output, is how far sales could fall before the plant stopped covering its costs, and that is precisely the question a lender will ask. And it is cheap and quick, which matters for a firm this size.
Where it is not: the analysis assumes ONE selling price, and this owner discounts above a hundred cases, so the revenue line is not straight and the real break-even point is to the right of 15,000 cases — the technique flatters the decision. It assumes costs split cleanly into fixed and variable, which holds for a month and not for the multi-year horizon a second line is bought over: across that period the rent and the equipment are choices too. It assumes everything made is sold, and a second line is precisely a bet that it will be. And it is static, while the decision is about several years.
Weighing them: the limitations bite hardest on exactly the decision being taken. A break-even point calculated monthly, at a single price, with output equal to sales, is a poor instrument for a multi-year investment in capacity — and the discounting means even the current figure understates the truth.
The recommendation follows from that. The owner should use break-even analysis, but as a SCREEN rather than as the decision: recalculate it at the average price actually achieved including discounts, and at the higher fixed costs the second line would bring, and treat the answer as the minimum the new capacity must sell. If that figure is close to or above what the market can absorb, the proposal fails on its own most optimistic test and no further work is needed. If it clears comfortably, the decision then needs the tools this analysis cannot supply — a cash-flow forecast over the period of the investment, and the sales forecast that underlies both. The most useful thing break-even analysis does here is tell the owner quickly whether the rest of the work is worth doing.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between sales volume and sales revenue?
flashcards.back: Volume is the number of units sold; revenue is what they sold for. Revenue = selling price × sales volume, so the two can move in opposite directions: 24,000 cases at $5.40 is more volume and more revenue than 20,000 at $6, and less profit.

flashcards.front: What makes a cost fixed rather than variable?
flashcards.back: Output. A fixed cost does not change when output changes — $36,000 of rent and salaries at zero cases and at 25,000. A variable cost changes directly with output: $3.60 a case. The split holds only for a stated period.

flashcards.front: How are total cost and average cost calculated?
flashcards.back: Total cost = fixed costs + total variable costs. Average cost = total cost ÷ output. At 20,000 cases: $36,000 + $72,000 = $108,000, and $108,000 ÷ 20,000 = $5.40.

flashcards.front: Why does average cost fall as output rises?
flashcards.back: The fixed cost is being divided by a bigger number. Variable cost per unit is $3.60 at every output; it is the $36,000 that thins — $3.60 a case at 10,000 and $1.44 at 25,000.

flashcards.front: Name four ways of improving sales volumes.
flashcards.back: Lower the price; widen distribution so the product reaches buyers who could not get it; change the product to suit buyers who had a reason not to buy; promote it to reach people who had not considered it. Two of the four cost money before any extra unit is sold.

flashcards.front: Why can improving sales revenue reduce profit?
flashcards.back: Revenue is price × volume, so a price cut moves both. The plant's cut to $5.40 raised revenue by $9,600 and each extra case carried $3.60 of variable cost, so profit fell from $12,000 to $7,200.

flashcards.front: What is a sales forecast and what is it for?
flashcards.back: An estimate of sales volume for a future period. It is the first figure in financial planning: it sets the materials ordered, the output break-even is compared against, the receipts line of the cash-flow forecast and the revenue line of the budget.

flashcards.front: What are the three factors affecting sales forecasts?
flashcards.back: Consumer trends — a lasting change in what buyers want. Economic variables — incomes, interest rates, exchange rates. Actions of competitors — their price, product, distribution or promotion. They do not all push the same way.

flashcards.front: Give four difficulties of sales forecasting.
flashcards.back: No history to forecast from: a product the market has not seen has no past sales to reason from, so the forecast rests on judgement. The factors move together: incomes, tastes and a competitor can all change in one quarter, and their effects do not simply add. The forecaster is not neutral: a forecast that has to justify a decision already taken is pulled towards the number that justifies it. Information costs money: a better forecast needs research, and the research has to be worth less than the error it removes.

flashcards.front: What is contribution and how is it calculated?
flashcards.back: Selling price − variable cost per unit: $6 − $3.60 = $2.40 a case. It is what each unit leaves towards the fixed costs once its own variable cost is paid. It is NOT profit per unit — nothing is profit until the fixed costs are covered.

flashcards.front: Define the break-even point.
flashcards.back: The output at which total fixed costs plus total variable costs equal total revenue, so the firm makes neither a profit nor a loss. For the plant, 15,000 cases: revenue $90,000 against costs of $36,000 + $54,000 = $90,000.

flashcards.front: How is the break-even point calculated from contribution?
flashcards.back: Fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit: $36,000 ÷ $2.40 = 15,000 cases. The division works because each unit pays its contribution towards the fixed costs, so the question is simply how many units cover $36,000.

flashcards.front: What is the margin of safety?
flashcards.back: Current or forecast output minus the break-even point, in units: 20,000 − 15,000 = 5,000 cases, which is 25% of output. It says how far sales can fall before the firm stops covering its costs.

flashcards.front: What happens to the break-even point if fixed costs rise?
flashcards.back: It rises, because the numerator is larger and contribution is unchanged. $42,000 ÷ $2.40 = 17,500 cases, up 2,500.

flashcards.front: What happens to the break-even point if variable cost per unit rises?
flashcards.back: It rises, and for a different reason: contribution falls, so the DIVISOR shrinks. At $4 a case, contribution is $2 and the break-even point is 18,000 cases.

flashcards.front: What happens to the break-even point if the selling price rises?
flashcards.back: It falls, because contribution rises. At $6.60 a case, contribution is $3 and the break-even point is 12,000 cases — down 3,000.

flashcards.front: How do you read a break-even chart?
flashcards.back: The revenue line starts at the origin and the total cost line starts at the fixed costs, $36,000. They cross at the break-even point. Left of the crossing the vertical gap is a loss, right of it a profit. The margin of safety is measured along the OUTPUT axis.

flashcards.front: Give four limitations of break-even analysis.
flashcards.back: One price for every case: the chart draws revenue as a straight line, so it cannot show a discount for a large order. Costs split cleanly in two: the split into fixed and variable is an assumption about the period, and a long enough period makes every cost variable. Everything made is sold: output and sales are the same axis on the chart, so unsold stock is invisible. A picture of one moment: the chart holds price and costs still, and the three change cases show how far the point moves when they do not.

flashcards.front: What are the five lines of a cash-flow forecast?
flashcards.back: Opening balance; receipts; payments; net cash flow (receipts − payments); closing balance (opening + net cash flow). The closing balance becomes the next month's opening balance, which is what makes it one forecast rather than separate months.

flashcards.front: Why are a month's receipts not the same as its sales?
flashcards.back: Because a forecast records money moving. With 30 days' credit, month 1's receipts are the PREVIOUS month's sales — $72,000 — while month 1's payments are for month 1's output.

flashcards.front: What does a negative closing balance mean?
flashcards.back: That the firm needs cash it will not have: an overdraft, a delayed payment or money from the owner. It is not a loss. The plant's trading is profitable in the month its balance reaches −$8,400; what moved was the timing of the money.

flashcards.front: Give three uses and three limitations of a cash-flow forecast.
flashcards.back: Uses: ask for finance early; time the spending you control; price the terms you offer. Limitations: the receipts are forecasts; a customer can pay late; it says nothing about why.

flashcards.front: What are the four purposes of a budget?
flashcards.back: Plan — a budget turns a target into figures a department can be given. Control — spending can be compared with the figure agreed, monthly, while there is time to act. Motivate — a figure somebody accepted is a target they own, which an instruction is not. Allocate — a fixed total forces a choice between the departments asking for it.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a historical and a zero-based budget?
flashcards.back: A historical budget starts from last period's actual figures and adjusts them: fast, and it carries the base forward unexamined. A zero-based budget starts every line at nothing and requires each amount to be justified: it tests the base, and it costs a great deal of time.

flashcards.front: What is a variance, and when is it favourable?
flashcards.back: The difference between a budgeted figure and the actual one. Favourable when it helps profit, adverse when it hurts it — so revenue above budget is favourable and cost above budget is adverse. Always a number AND a word.

flashcards.front: Why must variances be read together?
flashcards.back: Because they reconcile to the profit variance. The plant's month: revenue $9,600 favourable, variable costs $14,400 adverse, fixed costs $2,400 adverse — netting to $7,200 adverse on profit, in its best revenue month.

flashcards.front: Give four difficulties of budgeting.
flashcards.back: It is built on a forecast: a budget starts from a sales forecast and inherits chapter 2's difficulties. Spending to protect the allowance: a department that underspends can expect less next year. A target set too high demotivates: a figure nobody believes is a figure nobody works towards. It takes time to set: the meetings and the negotiation are a real cost, felt most by a small firm.

mistakes.title: Treating revenue as profit
mistakes.looks_like: "Revenue went from $120,000 to $129,600, so the price cut worked."
mistakes.why: Revenue is one side of the calculation. The extra 4,000 cases carried $3.60 of variable cost each, so total cost rose to $122,400 and profit fell from $12,000 to $7,200.
mistakes.instead: Whenever revenue moves, ask what happened to total cost. A route that improves revenue is worth having; it is not automatically worth taking.

mistakes.title: Sorting costs by the size or the timing of the payment
mistakes.looks_like: "Rent is monthly and large, so it is a fixed cost. Materials arrive weekly, so they are variable."
mistakes.why: The test is output, not the calendar. A monthly payment that rises with output is variable, and an annual one that does not is fixed. Getting this wrong puts the wrong figure in the contribution and every break-even answer after it is wrong.
mistakes.instead: Hold output at zero and ask whether the cost still has to be paid. If it does, it is fixed for that period.

mistakes.title: Reading contribution as profit per unit
mistakes.looks_like: "Contribution is $2.40 a case and we sold 20,000, so we made $48,000."
mistakes.why: Contribution is what each case leaves TOWARDS the fixed costs. Until the whole $36,000 is covered there is no profit at all. Profit at 20,000 cases is revenue less total cost: $120,000 − $108,000 = $12,000.
mistakes.instead: Use contribution for the break-even division. For profit, take revenue and subtract total cost.

mistakes.title: Drawing the total cost line from the origin
mistakes.looks_like: A break-even chart whose cost line and revenue line both start at zero output and zero money.
mistakes.why: At zero output the firm still owes its fixed costs, so the cost line has to begin at $36,000. A line from the origin makes the fixed costs disappear and puts the crossing in the wrong place — usually much too far left.
mistakes.instead: Mark the fixed cost level on the money axis first, then start the total cost line there and give it a gradient of the variable cost per unit.

mistakes.title: Giving the margin of safety in money
mistakes.why: That is the profit at the current output. The margin of safety is a quantity of OUTPUT: 20,000 − 15,000 = 5,000 cases, which is how far sales can fall before the firm is back at break-even.
mistakes.instead: Answer in units unless the question asks for the revenue or the profit at that output — and if it does, it will say so.

mistakes.title: Putting a credit sale on the receipts line in the month of the sale
mistakes.looks_like: A cash-flow forecast whose month 1 receipts are month 1's 20,000 cases at $6.
mistakes.why: A forecast records when money MOVES. With 30 days' credit, month 1's receipts are the previous month's sales, $72,000. Getting this wrong shifts every closing balance after it, because each one is carried forward.
mistakes.instead: Read the credit terms before filling in the receipts line, and check that the last closing balance is the opening balance plus every net cash flow.

mistakes.title: Reading a negative closing balance as a loss
mistakes.looks_like: "The forecast shows −$8,400 in month 2, so the plant is making a loss."
mistakes.why: A negative closing balance is a shortage of cash. The plant's trading in that month is unremarkable; what moved was the timing of the money. The forecast's job is to show that shortfall early enough for it to be arranged rather than survived.
mistakes.instead: Say "the plant will be short of cash" and name the month and the figure. Profitability is a different calculation on different figures.

mistakes.title: Reading favourable as good and stopping there
mistakes.looks_like: "Sales revenue was $9,600 favourable, so it was a good month."
mistakes.why: It was the best revenue month and the worse profit month. The extra cases were sold at a lower price and brought their variable costs with them, so $9,600 favourable less $14,400 and $2,400 adverse is $7,200 adverse on profit.
mistakes.instead: Read every line and check that the variances net to the profit variance. A favourable variance on one line is a question about the others, not a verdict.

chains.title: From a selling price to a margin of safety
steps: Take the selling price and the variable cost per case: $6 and $3.60. Both are per-unit figures and nothing can be worked out without them.
Subtract to get the contribution per case: $6 − $3.60 = $2.40. This is the part of each price that is available to pay the fixed costs.
Divide the fixed costs by the contribution: $36,000 ÷ $2.40 = 15,000 cases. That is the break-even point, and it is an output rather than an amount of money.
Subtract the answer from current output for the margin of safety: 20,000 − 15,000 = 5,000 cases, or 25% of what the plant makes.
chains.result: Every question in this chapter is one of those four steps or a change to one of the three figures the first step starts from. Change the price and step two changes; change the fixed costs and step three changes; change the output and only step four changes.

chains.title: From a sales forecast to an arranged overdraft
steps: Forecast the sales volume for each month. Nothing on the table can be filled in before the volume is estimated, and the estimate carries all four difficulties of forecasting.
Turn the sales into receipts using the credit terms. A sale becomes a receipt only when it is paid, so 30 days' credit moves each month's sales into the next month's receipts line.
Set the payments against each month's output. Payments follow what is PRODUCED, not what is collected — $36,000 fixed plus $3.60 a case.
Carry the closing balance into the next month. Opening plus net cash flow is the closing balance, and it becomes the next opening balance; this is the step that makes three months one forecast.
Arrange finance for the month the balance turns negative. The plant's reaches −$8,400, so the overdraft is arranged now rather than in the week it is needed.
chains.result: The forecast is worth building because of the last step. $8,400 known three months early is a negotiation; the same $8,400 discovered in the month it happens is an emergency.

chains.title: Why a price cut can raise revenue and lower profit
steps: The price falls from $6 to $5.40, so each case earns $0.60 less.
Volume answers: sales rise from 20,000 to 24,000 cases, a fifth more.
Revenue is price × volume, so the two effects net out: $5.40 × 24,000 = $129,600, up $9,600 on $120,000.
But every extra case brought $3.60 of variable cost with it, so total cost rose from $108,000 to $122,400.
Profit is revenue less total cost: $129,600 − $122,400 = $7,200, against $12,000 before.
chains.result: Revenue up $9,600, profit down $4,800 — and the break-even point moved too, from 15,000 to 20,000 cases, because contribution fell to $1.80. One decision, three figures, and they do not all point the same way.

chains.title: Why a rise in variable cost hurts more than the same rise in fixed cost
steps: Fixed costs rise by $6,000 a month. Contribution is untouched at $2.40, so only the numerator moves: $42,000 ÷ $2.40 = 17,500 cases, up 2,500.
Now instead let variable cost rise by $0.40 a case. Contribution falls to $2, so the DIVISOR shrinks.
The break-even point becomes $36,000 ÷ $2 = 18,000 cases, up 3,000.
At the plant's output the second change costs more: $0.40 × 20,000 = $8,000 a month against $6,000.
chains.result: A per-unit cost is multiplied by every case made, so its effect grows with output while a fixed cost's does not. That is why a firm negotiating hard on one of the two should usually negotiate on the variable one — and why the same $0.40 also turns the cash-flow forecast negative in all three months.

chains.title: How one wrong forecast reaches four decisions
steps: The sales forecast says 20,000 cases a month, and the three factors revise it to 16,200.
Materials are ordered against the forecast, months ahead, because the concentrate ships by sea — so a forecast that is too high is cash spent on stock that will not move.
The margin of safety is measured from it: at 16,200 cases it is 1,200 rather than 5,000, and the break-even point never moved.
The receipts line of the cash-flow forecast is the forecast turned into money, so a forecast wrong about the amount is usually wrong about the timing too.
The revenue line of the budget is the same figure, so every variance is measured against it.
chains.result: A variance measured against a forecast that was wrong tells the firm about its forecasting rather than about its performance. That is why the difficulties in chapter 2 matter more than the arithmetic in it.

evaluation.title: How much weight should a break-even point carry in a decision?
evaluation.content: Four questions, and the answer to the decision depends on all of them. Is there one selling price? The analysis draws revenue as a straight line, so a firm that discounts for large orders has a real break-even point to the right of the calculated one, and the technique flatters the decision. Over what period are the costs fixed? A break-even point calculated for a month is answering a monthly question; over the life of an investment the rent and the equipment are choices too, so the fixed costs in the numerator are not fixed at all. Is everything made being sold? Output and sales are the same axis on the chart, so unsold stock is invisible — which matters most when the decision being tested is an increase in capacity. And how far from the crossing is the firm now? A margin of safety of 25% means the analysis is describing a comfortable firm, and small errors in it change nothing; a margin of 7.4%, which is where the plant's revised forecast puts it, means the same errors decide the answer. Break-even analysis is at its most useful as a screen: recalculate at the price actually achieved and the costs actually expected, and if the proposal fails its own most optimistic test, no further work is needed.

evaluation.title: Which financial plan answers which question?
evaluation.content: Three tools and they are not interchangeable, so an answer that reaches for the wrong one has lost its marks before it starts. If the question is how much must be sold to cover the costs, or what one change to price or cost does to that figure, the tool is break-even analysis and the answer is an output. If the question is whether the firm will have the money to pay what it owes, and when, the tool is the cash-flow forecast and the answer is a closing balance in a named month — and the two answers can point different ways, which is the plant's own case: a comfortable 5,000-case margin of safety and a balance that reaches −$8,400. If the question is whether performance matched the plan and what to do about the gap, the tool is the budget and its variances, and the answer is a set of figures that must reconcile to the profit variance before any of them means anything. All three rest on the sales forecast, so all three inherit its difficulties — which is the one thing that is true of the whole topic and the most useful sentence to have ready for a twenty-mark question.

evaluation.title: Is a favourable variance good news?
evaluation.content: Not by itself, and the plant's month is the case worth remembering. Sales revenue beat its budget by $9,600 — the best revenue month it had — while profit missed by $7,200. Nothing was recorded wrongly: the extra cases were sold at $5.40 instead of $6 and each brought $3.60 of variable cost with it, so the favourable revenue variance and the $14,400 adverse cost variance are the same event seen from two lines. Three tests before calling any variance good news. Do the lines reconcile — does the favourable one less the adverse ones equal the profit variance? If not, something is missing from the table. What caused it — a variance won by discounting is a different fact from one won on volume at full price, and only the second is straightforwardly good. And was the budget itself sound: a favourable variance against a target set too low is a statement about the target. A variance is the start of a question. The answer is in the line beside it.
